newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy CPI slows to lowest rate for 28 years.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy CPI slows to lowest rate for 28 years.

text.p: Italian inflation slowed to its lowest level for 28 years in April, fuelling speculation in financial markets that the Bank of Italy may move to lower official interest rates soon.

Figures released by Italian statistics institute Istat on Tuesday showed consumer price increases slowed to 1.7 percent year on year last month compared with 2.2 percent in March -- the tamest rate of growth since April 1969.
The monthly rate for April was 0.1 percent, the same as March growth.

Italian bonds and futures climbed after the news, perceiving the data as increasing chances the Bank of Italy could lower the official discount rate 50 to 75 basis points in the near future. The discount rate stands at 6.75 percent and was last lowered in January this year.
"The markets are buoyant because people are speculating on the possibility of a cut," said Pio De Gregorio, economist at NatWest Markets in Milan.

Price growth has tailed off sharply in the last year, as shown by April 1996's rate of 4.5 percent. Economists say this is due to depressed domestic demand, the high cost of credit with a stronger lira and a favourable trend in international commodity prices.
Government ministers and industrialists have been calling for interest rates to be brought down but De Gregorio said he expected rate cut hopes to be disappointed near term.
"Clearly there is scope for an easing in monetary policy but the Bank of Italy would prefer to wait for the government's longer term budget plans and French election results," he said.
The centre-left government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi is due to present its three-year rolling plan of economic goals, known as the DPEF, by the end of May.

The DPEF sets out targets for inflation, economic growth and budget deficit levels and will be a guide to what steps the government intends to take in its endeavours to join and remain in European monetary union from its January 1999 start.
De Gregorio said French elections, due at the end of May and start of June, are also key to the outlook for Italian rates because a leftist victory could imply delay for monetary union.
This would cause turmoil in foreign exchange markets, upsetting the lira and preventing a central bank rate cut.

In London, Luca Jellinek, bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets, said: "I tend to think the Bank of Italy may wait until the end of this month, but it is a lottery and there are still hopes in the market of it happening sooner."

The government's goal for average inflation this year is 2.5 percent, compared with 3.9 percent in 1996, but many economists think consumer prices may actually come in slightly under target because of weak increases in the first quarter.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, quoted in a magazine interview recently, said recent inflation figures left room for interest rates to fall especially as he saw no motives for upward price pressure on the horizon.
"From the performance of wage inflation, the cost of raw materials, above all petrol, it is clear that the (inflationary) tendency is destined to last," Ciampi said.
